A further supplementary
question, Mr. Speaker. subtopic: BANK OF WESTERN CANADA-LOANS TO PREFERRED SHAREHOLDERS

speechtext:

the Treasury Board order to relieve this bank from the responsibilities which it led parliament to believe would in fact be carried out? The bank needed no encouragement with respect to any relief.

subtopic: BANK OF WESTERN CANADA-LOANS TO PREFERRED SHAREHOLDERS

Board minute underlined the conditions under which the Bank of Western Canada could operate. Nothing in any legislation is more restrictive. Those conditions carried out the wishes and intent of parliament, in accordance with the undertakings given by the corporation.

maintopic: VIET NAM-REQUEST FOR AID TO WAR VICTIMS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: VIET NAM-REQUEST FOR AID TO WAR VICTIMS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister will not be surprised if I question him today concerning the request of the Quakers in connection with medical supplies being made available to Viet Nam.

speakeroldname: Righi Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: VIET NAM-REQUEST FOR AID TO WAR VICTIMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to my hon. friend for his patience in this matter of a request from the Quakers that the government should provide free transportation for medical supplies to all parts of Yiet Nam, including of course North Viet Nam.
This matter was given the most careful and thoughtful attention by all those interested in and responsible for the conduct of Canadian aid programs, and I would emphasize that this is the context in which the Quakers' request had to be considered. As a result of this examination we came to the conclusion that we had no alternative but to decline the Quakers' request as inconsistent with the established practices of our official aid programs.
Specifically, the arrangements under which we work with recipient countries provide for the governments of these countries on their own account meeting the shipping charges on all goods or commodities supplied under Canada's official aid programs. Having insisted on this principle in our government to government aid programs, it would be difficult to adopt a different policy with respect to shipments from Canada of items provided by private groups interested in international aid programs. We have not done so in response to previous approaches from such groups, and such approaches have been made in the past.
Although that was the essence of the decision communicated to the Quakers yesterday, I might remind the house that there are no government obstacles in the way of normal shipments of medical supplies abroad. Similarly, if normal banking channels can be found for this purpose, we would place no obstacle in the way of transfer of funds for humanitarian purposes in Viet Nam.
February 7, 1967	COMMONS

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this time I should like to discuss the reform of the procedures of parliament. I want to take this opportunity of doing so because some excellent speeches have been made on this subject in various parts of the country, notably by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) and others. The resolution to set up a special committee to examine the continuation of the changed rules was passed by parliament without debate, and a good many of us had hoped to have an opportunity to discuss this matter at that time.
I have a fairly loud voice, Mr. Speaker, but I do find it very awkward and difficult to speak when about 87 other hon. members are speaking at the same time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. Will hon. members kindly continue their conversations behind the curtains? The hon. member for Royal has a most interesting speech to make which I am sure all of us would like to hear.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am particularly anxious that the government house leader, if he can spare a minute or two to listen to my speech, give me the benefit of his views at a later date because he and some other people share the responsibility for the fact that some ideas put forward by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) and others have not yet been translated into action.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question? Why does he single out the government house leader in this kind of personal reference when the government house leader is one of those in the house who try to obey the rules and conduct themselves in a responsible way?

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is what the hon. member said.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would soon use up my time if we are going to have a dichotomy of
February 7. 1967	COMMONS
views between us on this matter. I think that the minister has a responsibility and I respect the part he plays in the reform of the rules of parliament. However, among those of us who occupy the back benches there is a feeling that the recommendations for parliamentary reform that might have come from the minister have not as yet been indicated.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. I hope the hon. member will want to return now to the consideration of the business at hand. If so, he will not be charged with the last two or three minutes.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Of course the first reform that is essential is one that was recommended to parliament by the special committee on parliamentary procedure, and that was the establishment of a standing committee on procedures. I think it was a great pity that when certain changes were made to the rules this recommendation of the special committee was not carried out. The advantages of such a committee are, first, that owing to the fact that it would be a standing committee it would be established immediately upon the opening of parliament. It would also be able to keep under constant review many of the good changes that are being made in parliamentary institutions in other parts of the world.
I suggest that the reform of the procedures of this house should take place from top to bottom and that it has to be considered by a standing committee over several sessions perhaps. This is not a stop and start matter. It is a matter of a fundamental review which should take place over several years if we really mean what we say and are not just paying lip service to reform.
Parliamentary procedure boiled down to its simplest aspects has only two reasons. First of all, it enables the government to get its program through parliament. Second, it provides an opportunity for those who sit in opposition to the government to prevent the government from running the whole show. As a matter of fact we have had an excellent example recently of the effectiveness of parliamentary procedure during our long consideration of the transport bill. The original bill proposed to parliament was in no way comparable with the one which was finally enacted. I myself may criticize the length of the debate but I think the end result and the work of the 23033-8061
The Budget-Mr. Fairweather standing committee were a tribute to parliament and to those hon. members who participated in the eventual enactment of this legislation.
Money is the basis of our system and the control of the spending of money is really one of our main functions. There may be an easy control in that some people who take refuge in easy solutions to problems just say "No". In a way that is control. However, there is another way to control, the way which I believe parliament should follow. I refer to the examination of programs and policies. It seems to me that those of us who are members here should never lose an opportunity to discuss the working of parliament in other places because there are many people who think that our main function is to legislate and there are many people who have really set up what I might call a false god of legislation and have allowed emphasis upon legislation to supplant the control of spending.
Members of the parliament in Australia have brought about an interesting reform in their procedure. Perhaps it would be a little too fundamental for us yet although it needs the attention of the committee on procedure. I am referring to the change by which all major financial debates in Australia now occur during the various stages of the legislation. In other words, there is no committee of ways and means. Perhaps this is a drastic reform but Australia too is an offshoot of the mother of parliaments and it has seen fit to adopt this procedure. From what I read it has not meant that the rights of members to comment, criticize and exercise control have been inhibited in any way.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
There was a tragic example not so long ago in connection with the pay of civil servants. I believe this is an occasion where parliament goes too far. I do not believe that the withholding of supply should be pushed to the limit so that a man who works for the government may be without his properly earned salary.
There is another reform which I should like to be considered and that is the allocation of time for debate. I believe that the special government proposal in this connection was the result of a compromise and is therefore much too complicated. I think a better way would be for the operations of the house to be a matter of day to day negotiation between the whips and house leaders to a greater
12738	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Fairweather extent than I am informed they have been up to now.
With great respect to the Speaker, I feel that the question period should undergo drastic reform. I am not saying that because something is done in Britain it is good. Obviously the geographic area of Britain and the fact that Britain has a national press make it easier to have a more disciplined question period than we have. However, I feel it would be a great reform to have to give 48 hours notice of questions. I believe that the Leader of the Opposition, as an officer of the house, should have the opportunity without notice to ask a question of the Prime Minister or a minister each day.
The fact that the order paper is cluttered with hundreds of questions makes it a poor thing. There is no such cluttering of the order paper in Britain. If there is not time to answer questions on orders of the day, written replies are sent promptly. In this way there is no back-up of questions. I feel sure this procedure would be welcomed not only by those who produce the documents but by those of us who have to wait weeks and sometimes even months to get answers to written questions.
In September, in another part of this building, one of the committees of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Conference considered the problem of parliamentary reform. It interested me to find that there was no parliamentary representative from anywhere in the Commonwealth who did not feel that some aspect of the parliamentary system could undergo fundamental revision. One of the British members set out his views quite succinctly and perhaps at this point of my speech I may share his comments with you on the real reason for parliament. I refer to the remarks of Mr. Daniel Awdry, a member of parliament in the United Kingdom. He said that parliament is the assembly which provides the government and, incidentally, the Prime Minister, to the nation.
The next function of parliament, he said, is to control the executive and, of course, control of the nation's money is at the heart of our parliamentary system. However, he said that the truth today is that control of spending by the House of Commons is largely nonexistent. No one in this chamber could say that comment does not apply to this place as well. The third function that Mr. Awdry suggests is one of information. He said:
It is the duty of parliament and parliamentarians to create new ideas, to produce original thought and to pass information on to the electors-

DEBATES	February 7, 1967
Finally, Mr. Awdry believes that it is the function of parliament to pass laws. It interested me to note that in his catalogue the passage of legislation was last. I know that the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Turner) would take a keen interest in the third function of parliament, that is, information and the creation of new ideas because he and a good many of us share the view that from the conception of an idea to its eventual enactment, or even first of all its discussion, there is a trail that even the most careful explorer would find difficult in tracking to its end. I think this is tragic and I believe it is part of the reason for the declining respect for members of parliament and their role as initiators.
It has been my experience, and I hope I can say this objectively and modestly, that when we are in a forum where we can share ideas with people they seem to be, first of all, amazed that members of parliament have ideas. Once they get over their amazement they are quite pleasantly surprised to find that some members of parliament are reasonable. The third source of wonder they express is, why can you not do something about these things? Most of the forums I have attended have not sufficient time in their programs to allow members to tell these people why it is so difficult to translate an idea into eventual action by the government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member if he would not agree that it is very difficult to make headlines out of an idea?

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am accused sometimes of being a cynic but I am not really cynical about the reform of parliament. I know quite well that a speech on parliamentary reform, made at 3.30 on an afternoon when other events in this building will get headlines, is not likely to get much attention from the press. This does not disturb me one bit. I think ideas are worth sharing. I hope that government members, including the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Stewart), will join issue on some of the things I have been saying.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I ask the hon. gentleman another question? I do not believe I want to join issue with him on many of his statements, but does he not insist that the problem to which he is now referring, the problem of better public discussion in our democracy, is really one which encompasses far more than improving debate in this house?
February 7, 1967

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, and I could attempt to show why by having a discourse here or somewhere else about it but my time is rapidly moving along. Obviously one of the functions which would stand high in my list of the functions of parliament would be the sharing and gathering of information. It is for this reason I really have not too much respect for those who say the duty of a member is to sit in this chamber day in and day out for 200 or. 300 days a year. I think that is a sacred cow that is trotted out whenever it is convenient. A member who is able to get around the country comes here better prepared for debate.
The restructuring of our committee system as recommended to parliament by the committee on procedure would have worked better than the one that was finally set before us by the government. It was the feeling of those of us who served on that committee that there should really be no more than 15 committees of parliament with fewer rather than more members. This would make them more efficient. We now have 21 committees, if I am properly informed, each with 24 members. Today is probably a good example of how impossible the system is when ten committees are sitting. As a matter of fact, I am on two committees that have meetings called for 3.30 this afternoon and it is now 3.40,
I believe that the quorums of committees could be greatly reduced without any harm, particularly for those committees which in the early part of their agenda are receiving a large number of briefs. It is apparently assumed that a great many members do not take the trouble to read briefs. Perhaps if the quorums were reduced and more attention were paid to the preparation and reading of briefs, committee work would move along a bit faster.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
There are two reforms I should like to mention which have been adopted by the United Kingdom parliament and I think would be helpful to us. One concerns what is known as the early day motion, which is a system whereby members representing the various parties sometimes set down a motion in order to test public opinion on issues, thus giving a particular matter publicity, as the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough mentioned earlier. If the matter is serious enough an opportunity is given to the opposition or to those members who want to press the motion to have a day set aside for debate.
The Budget-Mr. Fairweather
I feel that this proposal is an important one. I notice that it was used recently when 70 or 80 members of the British House of Commons put their names on an early day motion which deplored the fact that the government was raising fees for foreign students from outside the United Kingdom who were studying there. These 70 or 80 members were not necessarily supporters of the government; they represented the various parties in the house. I think many more opportunities should be given for that type of challenge to policy.
Another reform which, though in the embryo stage, I think would be worth while considering is that known as the second reading committee. Those of you who read the Observer will know that Mr. Richard Crossman has recently been discussing the second reading committee concept. I should like to refer to an article by Mr. Rudolf Klein entitled "Mr. Crossman's New Time-saver" which appeared in the January 29 edition of the Observer:
Crossman's basic idea is simple. Ministers want "certainty and predictability" in getting their measures through the Commons. Backbenchers want more opportunity to influence government policy. Here, he believes, are all the makings of a possible deal, since "business-like predictability is worth paying for."
In other words, Mr. Speaker, if the government could be sure of a legislative pattern it should be prepare to make certain days available for debate on issues that the opposition members feel should take place
To return to the second reading committee proposal, I point out that this committee processes bill which both parties in the United Kingdom-in the case of Canada it would be all parties-agree are non-controversial. The article states:
It is a system which could gradually give greater influence to backbench M.P.'s while leaving the government's power of initiative intact. For instance, during all the long hours devoted to the steel bill, M.P.'s never once discussed how the steel industry is going to be organized under state ownership.
I do not want to apply the steel bill example to Canada, but I do not think it will take much imagination on the part of hon. members to realize that this type of thing happens all too often in this chamber. In other words, although legislation is debated the ultimate result of the legislation is rarely given any meaningful consideration.
The report which instituted the second reading committee in the United Kingdom was made to parliament on March 25, 1965, so
12740	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Fairweather that they have had a year or so to test this system. An examination of our order paper discloses that there are many non-controversial bills which would receive better attention if they were referred to a committee such as the second reading committee. In our experience it often happens that at the end of a day the house leaders are able to arrange for certain items to be brought forward, and usually the house takes an ambitious initiative and passes them very quickly without any consideration at all. A second reading committee would mean that these non-controversial items would have some attention.

speechtext: That is before or after second reading?

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague has asked a most interesting question. This is done before second reading. I understand that in all cases the actual second reading is left to parliament itself. In other words, parliament can either accept or reject the recommendation for second reading made by this committee, so that parliament's rights are properly protected.
My reading of literature on parliamentary reform tells me, Mr. Speaker, that two rather simple steps have been taken. The first one was in the early 1880's the other in 1902. Until the 1880's it had been felt that parliament should be untrammelled and everyone bowed to freedom of speech and other shibboleths. Parliament had to face an interesting group of members from Ireland who used every device and delaying action to hold up parliament. As is usual when challenged, parliament found a means of using freedom of speech to its proper end. In other words, Mr. Speaker, these proposals have had historical origins, and I am intrigued to think that the trouble encountered by the Irish M.P.'s really instituted the first great procedural reform in the British House of Commons.
However, we in Canada have not had that experience so our rules, with very little variation, are the rules that we adopted prior to the reforms which took place in Britain in the 1880's. There are, of course, certain exceptions, and we can all think of them. That is why I plead with the government to take the initiative in re-establishing as a standing committee the committee on procedure, because reform is not a matter that should be handled piecemeal.
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, if reform is to be anything more than just a matter for discussion by members of parliament

DEBATES	February 7, 1967
throughout the country we should examine the fundamental reasons behind each and every one of our rules. Perhaps a case can be made, as it was made in Australia, for abandoning the committee of ways and means procedure. Perhaps a case can be made for, shall I say, having a slightly more disciplined question period. Perhaps a case can also be made-I think it can

for reducing the number of members on committees, reducing the quorums, and widening the scope of the responsibilities that those committees are called upon to undertake.
In last month's issue of "Encounter" there is an article by Mr. Henry Fairlie. In it we are reminded of a phrase used by Mr. R. A. Butler-"the patience of politics". Mr. Fairlie
says:
The phrase is R. A. Butler's. It expresses, more vividly than any other single phrase, the character of politics in a free country.
In the politician, it demands that he should accustom himself to the inevitable fluctuations of political fortunes; that he should And defeat and failure only an invitation to renewed efforts; that he should overcome the galling frustrations of enforced idleness and opposition, and be able to look forward to ten years in the wilderness with equanimity and self-assurance.
That is something from which a good many of us would profit if we took it to heart.
It demands that he should never try to seize imaginary initiatives or seek speedy results; that he should wait calmly for his opportunity; that he should never despair or panic.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
It demands that he should bear obloquy, misrepresentation, and injuries without complaint; that he should expect no gratitude; that he should remain silent when one word would justify him, if that word would injure his cause. Above all, It demands that he should never, whatever the provocation, cease to trust in the right instincts of a free people; that he should believe always In their ability, in the long run, to distinguish truth from falsehood, justice, from injustice, the sound from the meretricious; that he should, in this belief, patiently pursue the task of bringing different ideas and interests into contact with each other, never doubting that the arts of a free government are among the most rewarding of all the arts of a civilised people.
We have a responsibility to so enlarge the scope of this chamber and the character, if I may use that word, and attributes of its members that our people may indeed believe we are good practitioners of the art of politics.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it should be recalled that the whole tenor and philosophy of the March, 1966 budget, which met with general approval, was one consistent with a burgeoning economy showing danger
February 7, 1967

signs of unrestrained growth. That anti-inflationary budget contained provisions designed to prolong prosperity without dire inflationary price spirals, exacting hardship on low and fixed income segments of our society. Among other things the moderate income tax increases on medium and upper incomes and the judicious decrease on low incomes, the elimination and postponement of certain capital projets and the progressive removal of the 11 per cent sales tax on production equipment and machinery, contributed to maintaining our spectacular boom. 1 felt at that time that the finance minister deserved the highest commendation for coolly and efficiently introducing a reasonable budget, with some unpalatable provisions, designed to achieve for all our citizens full employment and sustained or increased purchasing power enabling them to live in comfort and security in this prosperous land.
It has been generally conceded and the Economic Council of Canada has endorsed the view that the economy at present is rather delicately balanced. There is a strong suspicion that it is heading for a slowdown. No economist can say with exactitude the precise inclination of our economy. I suggest that the minister, with commendable alertness, has kept a constant protective vigil. Now, based on statistics and the best economic opinions available, he has introduced a realistic budget which should maintain the intricate balance between inflation and recession so essential to the material well-being of all Canadian citizens.
This budget, designed to make no radical impact on our economy, makes provision for raising sufficient funds to pay for the guaranteed income supplement for our senior citizens. Parliament, representing the wishes of the people, has provided a new revolutionary concept in the guaranteed income plan for our senior citizens. This plan without a means or needs test, as opposed to a flat increase of $25 a month, will provide some half million of Canada's old age pensioners with $60 a year more than the Conservative and N.D.P. flat rate proposal would have provided. What is most important, the guaranteed income supplement, unlike the flat $25 a month increase, is weighted in favour of those on low and modest incomes. In effect the government has not raised the pension for people in high income brackets but has provided for increases for older people who definitely need * supplement to their incomes to live in security and dignity in a land to which they have contributed so much.
The Budget-Mr. Tolmie
These additional payments to pensioners are expected to cost the federal treasury between $260 million and $280 million. The government, after reviewing all the possibilities of raising the required funds to pay for this very necessary and worth-while plan, decided to raise the maximum amount payable by an individual by reason of the 4 per cent tax on personal income under the Old Age Security Act from $120 a year to $240 a year. This increased tax only affects those taxpayers with taxable income exceeding $3,000 after all exemptions and deductions. In effect the result is that a married taxpayer with two children will not have an increase unless he is earning more than $5,700 a year, which is well above the current national average of wage earnings. Significantly, the tax increase will not affect two thirds of our present income taxpayers. In addition, the general sales tax was increased from 11 per cent to 12 per cent, but it should be emphasized that this increase will not apply to building materials and will not affect the cost of food, fuel and services exempt from this tax.
It is self-evident that funds must be provided for this novel and enlightened guaranteed income concept, and I submit that these budget proposals achieve this as neatly and fairly as possible. Fiscal and monetary policies are for most of us lofty concepts; often they are dull and incomprehensible. These Policies are formulated by brilliant, intellectual experts with charts, computers and statistics. They are instruments to be played for our material welfare, and the tune to be produced depends on many complex and variable interlocking economic factors.
There is, however, one factor which we can all understand, the rising cost of living. Though inextricably bound with general economic conditions, living costs are amenable to diagnosis and prescriptions for at least a partial cure can be applied. Here the government can play a role. Happily it has taken a commendable step in setting up the Senate and House of Commons joint committee on consumer affairs. No one pretends that this is the complete answer to the rising cost of living as painfully revealed in high food prices, but if the consumer, which is every man, woman and child in this nation, is being unfairly exploited by dubious business practices and exorbitant profits such a committee can reveal this and suggest remedial legislation to prevent the continuance of such abuses. Frankly, I feel that the very fact our large food suppliers know their operations are subject to public scrutiny will make them loath

February 7. 1967
The Budget-Mr. Tolmie to pursue practices inimical to the best interests of their customers. There has been some indication that since the formation of this committee certain prices in some categories have decreased. Quite conceivably some of this decrease could be attributed to the work of the committee.
Emerging from all economic theory, one stark fact remains. Our present and future wealth and well-being depend upon our productivity and the preservation and enhancement of our national resources. My thesis is simple. All policies and factors which increase the productivity of this nation and husband and strengthen our national resources eventually add to our total economic health. Preservation of our water resources through war on pollution, the improvement of the general health of the nation through the passage of the medicare bill, more liberalized and enlightened immigration policies, social reform-all these contribute to our wealth. These influences are less easy to gauge and assess as factors affecting our affluence, but though not as discernible they are real and quietly and unobstrusively play a significant role in the improvement of our economy.
What is the point of manipulating economic levers if we neglect to preserve and increase the source of our wealth? By and large, our policies in respect of water, land, minerals and forests have been enlightened and constructive. However, one of our irreplaceable and basic resources, our water, is in jeopardy. In dire straits are our great lakes with their treasures of fish, matchless beaches and residential shores attracting millions of tourist dollars and providing rest, relaxation and peace of mind for thousands of our citizens.
What is shocking is that for years there has been a continuous insidious deterioration of these assets because of water pollution, and until quite recently few, if any, steps had been taken to prevent this vicious onslaught. In December, 1965, the International Joint Commission issued a most disturbing report on pollution in the great lakes in which it practically stated that lake Erie was fast becoming a large septic tank and an open venomous sewer. It stated that algae growths curtail commercial fishing and recreational activities, impart obnoxious odours, impair filtering operations of industrial and munic,-ipal water treatment plants, lower waterfront property values and generally threaten destruction of the lakes as a valuable water resource. Certain recommendations

were made urging the Canadian and American governments, in association with state and provincial governments, to take action to ensure that industries refrain from dumping chemical wastes into our great lakes, that municipalities be forced to treat their sewage properly and that an accelerated program of research into the baffling causes of water pollution be instituted.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
It is always most difficult to get action in fields of jurisdiction divided among the United States government, the federal government, the provincial government and municipal governments and consequently there has been a welter of confusion and ambiguity as to the progress we are making in the war on pollution. In order to erase any lingering suspicion that nothing has been done by the federal government, it should be noted that among other things the following measures have been taken. At present there is a massive research program endeavouring to ascertain the baffling causes of pollution. Three important federal agencies, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Fisheries Research Board are combining forces, with each agency contributing money and scientists to conduct special studies for which they are best qualified. For part of the program the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources has chartered the 136-foot stern trawler, Braudel. The department has fitted out this modern vessel as a survey and research ship and it has been working out of Kingston, Ontario. Two 30-foot launches will be employed in the national health and welfare departmental program.
Under contract with the federal government, the great lakes institute will be making co-ordinated studies in lake Ontario and lake Erie. A research laboratory on pollution will be constructed at Burlington, Ontario. Over $1.5 million was invested in this study of the lower lakes in 1966 and 90 per cent of the cost has been borne by the federal government. This investment will grow from year to year, reaching an estimated level of over $5 million by 1970.
This intensive survey program is only one facet of the total federal effort, and it is not generally recognized how large the federal government contributions have been toward the installation of sewage treatment facilities. Over $200 million has been advanced as loans by the federal government for this purpose at
February 7, 1967

a low rate of interest and with a lengthy amortization period. Over $50 million of these loans will be forgiven as part of a special arrangement for the encouragement of such construction. The federal government has also contributed through its winter works program which supports, among other projects, the installation of sewage systems and treatment plants. It is estimated, for example, that at least $17 milhon of federal funds has been contributed to the construction of these installations and systems in Ontario alone.
The federal government has made special concessions to assist companies to instal improved treatment facilities. The income tax regulations have been amended to permit a fast write-off of the capital cost of these installations. It should also be noted that the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources has been reorganized so that one special branch will have jurisdiction over water pollution. In addition, the council of federal and provincial resource officials is constantly studying this problem and they will shortly make recommendations to their respective governments. I mention these steps to indicate that the government has not by any means been indifferent to the menace of water pollution. However, in my opinion the situation is now so serious that even greater efforts must be made. A veritable crash program is required immediately if we are going to preserve this most prized national resource.
One of our greatest resources, of course, is the number and quality of our people, and our immigration policies have a tremendous impact upon our future growth and prosperity. The government has indicated in its white paper on immigration that it proposes to implement a more liberal immigration policy consistent with the needs and demands of a young and growing country. Personally, I favour a broad, liberalized immigration policy based not only on the economic advantages but for social and humanitarian reasons. Skilled manpower is urgently needed at the present time. Expanding industry is pleading not only for skilled tradesmen but for unskilled workers who can be trained. If we are to sustain our economic expansion, if we are going to push ahead to new frontiers, if we are going to realize the potential explosive power of this lusty giant which is only barely flexing its biceps, if we are to realize our manifest destiny of becoming one of the richest nations on earth, if we ever hope to decrease our dependency on the United States and avoid a satellite status vis-a-vis that
The Budget-Mr. Tolmie country, then we must encourage the regulated flow of new Canadians to this country, who in turn are producers and consumers alike.
We have water in abundance, minerals, lumber, oil and farmlands. The only resource not in ample supply is people. To cite an example, does it not seem incongruous in a new and developing nation at this time in our history when one realizes that instead of considering additional rail transportation across this land one transcontinental train was cancelled because allegedly there were not enough people to use it? With more people we could not only have presented the cancellation of the "Dominion," with all the attendant inconvenience and hardship, but the annual C.N.R. debt, running into the millions, could be reduced. We must welcome these people as Canadians have always welcomed new immigrants. We need their skills, their know-how, their enthusiasm. We need their purchasing power and their consuming power. We need all the positive things they can contribute.
This does not mean we open our portals wide and encourage an uncontrolled influx beyond our national capacity to absorb. We must be sure that we do not allow our immigration policies to impose added burdens on our unemployment situation, our housing or our social welfare facilities. I believe that we must welcome these people for other reasons less selfish, less pragmatic and less definable. We have a gigantic country beckoning for people to fill it, tremendous expanses untouched, soil to be tilled, minerals to be mined. We must welcome people because we have a wonderful country and a splendid way of life which we should share with those less fortunate. We have a duty to mankind to embrace other peoples of the world and allow them to share with us the opportunities and promise this happy land provides. My riding is a good example of an area where people from all races have mingled and enriched each other with their respective customs and cultures. This all makes an interesting and refreshing mosaic of life and adds vibrancy and colour to any community. This same dynamic pattern of growth can be emulated throughout Canada, adding sparkle and zest to our national life.
The most crucial factor in productivity is, of course, the industry, talents and efficient output of our people. The added energy and drive of a well adjusted, happy people, unhampered by nagging social and domestic problems, can add immeasurably to our total
February 7, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Tolmie wealth as this increased unleashed productive capacity is infused into our national economy. Apart from all humanitarian considerations, reforms in many spheres can improve the vitality of this young nation.
This government has provided a glittering array of social welfare programs, unsurpassed in our parliamentary history. I feel that as we enter our centennial year there should be a shifting of emphasis to social reforms which not only would relieve abuses, inequities and human misery and could be effected without plundering the treasury but would, in relevance to a budget debate, strengthen the economic sinews of this nation. We have made a good start. The introduction of medicare will eventually ensure, through the improved health of our nation, a continued and more rapid exploitation of our full productive capacities. We are in effect husbanding and fostering the growth of our greatest national resource, the health of our people.
Highway accidents exact a staggering financial toll. The curtailment of this wanton destruction of life and property is a most direct way to contribute significantly to our material well-being. I strongly advocate, as one way to fight this plague on the national level, the introduction of a national safety code making it mandatory for automobile companies to instal certain minimum safety features in all automobiles built or sold in Canada. I admit that there are inherent constitutional problems involved but I submit that they can be circumvented, and in the national interest this type of legislation should not be delayed.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Our divorce laws are generally conceded to be savage, unrealistic, archaic, completely inconsistent with prevailing philosophies and crying out desperately for change. As a lawyer I have seen the human misery and degradation caused by cruel divorce laws. As a member of parliament I have received more poignant, pitiful and heartrending pleas for changes in this domestic field than in any other sphere of human relations. In a civilized country which prides itself on its enlightened views on the great social questions of the day, this cancer has been allowed to grow and thrive for a hundred years of our history, gnawing at the very vitals of our social fabric.
At least this government, for the first time in the history of the country, appointed a joint committee of the house and Senate to investigate divorce reform, and it is painfully

probing this pathetic picture of human misery. Frankly, I think it is time we got a recommendation from that committee, and then the government should take immediate action and bring about a realistic broadening of the grounds for divorce consistent with our existing domestic realities and attitudes. I would like to see divorce reform passed during our centennial session because 1967 could be a commemorative year signalling the end of 100 years of human bondage. I can think of no more worth-while centennial project for our centennial session. Relevant to a budget debate, the peace of mind, the renewed interest in life and the happier social adjustment afforded by divorce reform would release a well of human energy, long stultified and dormant, which would pour forth into our life stream, adding renewed vigour and strength to our entire nation.
A genuine attack on hate literature, which demoralizes and saps the will and strength of many segments of our society, would, by dissipating neuroses and anxieties, again release latent energies which could add strength and vitality to our national economic life. A joint Senate and House of Commons committee is studying the question of hate literature and I would hope that an early report will recommend effective action against this concealed, insidious but nonetheless devasting social disease.
In summary I say this. We have the economic weapons to promote material wellbeing-a consumer committee, fiscal and monetary policies as enunciated in our budget-but we must keep constantly in mind one salient fact, that our real wealth resides in the natural resources of this land and the energies of our people. In this our centennial year, by social reforms based on humanitarian concepts and social justice, we must also release the explosive energies and talents of our people to their fullest potential. In this way and in this way only will we ensure lasting prosperity.
In this our centennial year we should give prayerful thanks for the rich blessings of this gracious and bountiful land, but should be ever mindful of the needs of every segment of our society and must ensure that all of our people share fairly in the almost limitless largesse of this proud nation. On our one hundredth birthday a dazzling vista of golden opportunities unfolds before us. A much blessed nation, proud, and master of its own destiny, with eager hope peers ahead into a
February 7, 1967

warm, bright and glowing future. How fortunate we are today to share in this great dream.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I represent the great agricultural district of Athabasca and in the short time at my disposal I want to repeat a warning to this house and to the government in particular that agriculture will remain the backbone of Canada as long as we have a country. There are a great many experts in agriculture today, even in the farm unions, who are giving up hope of retaining the family farm. Sometimes through lack of vision and leadership the government finds it is necessary to impose quotas and hold prices down, rather than up, because a support price at a low level across the board can tend to force farmers to enlarge their farms and increase their production in the vain hope of closing the cost-price gap. I take an entirely different view.
I think that if we concentrate on markets, principally markets abroad, and instead of asking farmers to increase their acreage and buy out their neighbours, ask them to become efficient on their own small acreage, these are the only answers to the problem of maintaining a large and happy rural life in Canada.
The small farms in Quebec, the maritimes and Ontario are being harder hit now than ever before. They are no longer able to compete in the labour market for skilled operators of machinery, especially since farm labourers are not covered by unemployment insurance. On two occasions we have introduced private bills dealing with this problem but have had no success in having it rectified by the government.
The small family farm cannot operate without help. The young people who are expected to stay at home seek, if not direct wages, that the family farm be put on a paying basis. I am not one to get up and criticize government policies without making specific suggestions. I have made some previously and I do not hesitate to do so again.
I believe we are ignoring a tremendous market for meat products, particularly in Asia. When it was difficult to sell Asians our grain because they said they did not have the money, we decided to sell them grain on a time basis and by doing so we opened up a whole new vista for agriculture in western Canada which had the grain to sell. So far we have not even explored the possibility of selling meat products to Asia. The purchasing power of Asian countries is low. They do not have American dollars and are forced to buy
The Budget-Mr. Bigg from us with sterling. Our job should be to consult with financial experts and find some way to give purchasing power to Asia. On this narrow issue hangs the whole future not only of the agricultural industry of Canada but possibly of the peace of the world.
We should send trade missions not only to Asia but to every other corner of the world and find out intelligently what the rest of the world wants that we can produce. Canada is one of the few countries left in the world with virgin land. We can still plow new land in Canada. Most of the old countries of the world, particularly the over-populated ones, have worn-out soil. But in Canada we still have new land, and in western Canada new potash deposits are being developed.
Certainly Asia and the underdeveloped countries of the world cannot pay for many of our products, but we shall have to find some way of financing purchases for them. When we go abroad to sell a product such as potash we should use the combined brains of a number of industries. From the point of view of being able to sell pork to China, have we considered the possibility of renovating old steel drums from the oil industry, which are no longer capable of carrying high naphtha products but are still capable of being used for the shipment of products like canned meat and fruit? We might line the barrels with an inch or two of petroleum wax. Backward countries do not yet have electricity and in a place like China the people could convert the barrel linings into candles. We could ship our meat in steel, aluminum or plastic pails. The peasant people of Asia could use the pails for irrigation purposes or for household needs and thus we could sell them two products in one.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I know that the price of pork or any other meat or fruit product when shipped across the Pacific is likely to be prohibitive unless we employ all our know-how in providing proper containers for the food when it is being sent there. By this means we will be able to help them increase their standard of living and thus help them get on their feet so that they can afford the high standard of living to which they are as much entitled as we are.
The former administration took up this matter very seriously. The idea was not received with deaf ears on the part of the government headed by the then prime minister and so ably assisted by the hon. member

February 7, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Bigg for Northumberland (Mr. Hees) in the Department of Trade and Commerce. There was a deficit of several hundred million dollars in 1956-57 but when we left office we had a favourable trade balance of $1,300 million. I note with some horror that we have now slipped back to a position even worse than that in which we were in 1957. The estimated trade deficit this year is approximately $2 billion, or three times as high as it was in 1957. This is not wholly the fault of any one department.
I suggest that in 1967 at least those people who are making money and are able to balance their own budgets should think about staying at home and spending here the $800 million or $900 million currently being spent abroad. Let us make our centennial year a successful one financially. We can do this simply by staying home and spending this $1 billion here. This would cut our deficit in half. In order to buy Canada back let us buy Canadian products. I shall not speak of tax incentives for they are there already. The Canadian people should wake up to the fact that it pays to invest in Canada. If they would do this and take advantage of the existing tax incentives we could reduce the unfavourable balance of trade still further.
I suggest to the Department of Trade and Commerce that as a publicity stunt they might mark clearly all Canadian products which are produced by Canadian owned corporations. The percentage to which these companies are Canadian owned could be marked on the cans containing their products. This could be done by using coloured bands. By the size of the maple leaf and the colour of the band on the can, one would know the extent to which the product was Canadian when buying it in a store. In the affluent society of which we are so proud we should make sure that a very large percentage of the money we spend remains at home. A sensible way in which to buy Canada back is to buy things made in Canada. We cannot afford to make things in Canada unless we buy them when they are made.
I think that the subject of taxation is a good place to bring up a favourite suggestion of mine again. I have in mind the problem of double taxation. In the somewhat tax free province of Alberta one pays as much as $600 or $700 a year in taxes on an ordinary six-room house. There is no exemption whatsoever from income tax in this respect. In the United States mortgage payments are deleted from taxable income. I suggest that we might

take a lead in this regard from our great neighbour to the south and do away with what I call double taxation as applied to householders. The whole burden of education is carried by those who own their own homes or, worse still, by those who are trying to buy their own homes under one of the existing mortgage plans. This is unfair. It is inequitable and actually it makes the purchase of a new home at present prices almost an impossibility for the average wage earner.
I think that centennial year would be a good time to set up the Indian claims commission. This is something which has been promised ever since the treaties were signed. If the Indian claims commission were established, the Indians would have a forum in which to air their complaints. The Indian claims commission could decide once and for all whether or not we have kept the treaties with the Indians. Perhaps it would be able to determine whether or not the twentieth century interpretation we have made of these treaties is an adequate one.
Those who are our first citizens should be given their proper place in this country. I notice with some satisfaction that the efforts made particularly by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Fane) have borne fruit. The Indian reserves at Saddle Lake and Goodfish Lake are getting electrification. They have waited a long time for this. I congratulate anyone who has had anything to do with this. In this twentieth century the Indian people are just as entitled to the amenities of life as we are. Now they will be able to wash their clothes, light their homes, study and enjoy themselves.
For too long a time the Indian affairs branch has taken a paternalistic attitude toward the Indian people. I suggest that the sooner we fill the Indian affairs branch either with Indians or with persons who have a first hand working knowledge of Indian problems, the sooner we will be able to improve the lot of the Indians. There is no point in educating one Indian and then sending him back to the reserve to become submerged in the hopeless task of trying to raise the standard of living of the people there. We must direct a mass attack on the Indian problem. As I say, we will accomplish nothing until the initiative which the Indians have to a marked degree is encouraged to the point where they can be put in charge of their own affairs. I have seen drafts of one or two of the bills to set up this commission. One of the proposals is that the Indian appointees on the commission could be
February 7, 1967

removed at the whim of the government. In one case it was suggested that this could be done by a joint order by the two houses of parliament. I do not care from whom the orders come. The Indian appointees to the commission must be responsible to the Indian people and to the Indian people alone; otherwise it would be better not to have any such commission because it would not be respected by the Indians. It would be something which would drive the Indians farther back rather than bring them ahead.
I am pleased also that something is being done about housing. There is no point in building shells of houses on Indian reserves and then expecting the Indians to finish them. The houses which are built for the Indians should be ready to be occupied. They should be equipped with proper doors, windows, heating equipment and everything else that is necessary so they can live in the extreme climate in which most Indian people live. It is absolutely a waste of time and money to build a shell of a house in which these people have to sleep on the floor. If these houses are not warm and comfortable the Indian people will not sleep in them. They will move back to the tent which has been the Indian's home for generations and they will keep themselves warm in the manner to which they have become accustomed for thousands of years. They will live in these tents and rip the lath off the walls and the shingles off the roofs of the houses so they will have firewood to keep themselves warm. Where the Indian people have had a chance they have measured up in every way to their brethren of European origin.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
We have just passed the omnibus transportation bill which portends strange things for the future of railroading. Let me refer again to the vision of the former administration which built lines such as the one to Thompson in northern Manitoba and the Pine Point line in the Northwest Territories. I never thought this was a gamble, as did some others, and it has paid off magnificently. Instead of busily considering where lines should be abandoned we should be considering where new ones may be built.
I have in my hand a map indicating proposed rail line abandonments. One need only look at it to see the great need for railway facilities in certain areas. Let me remind the house again of a promise made by
The Budget-Mr. Bigg many governments to the people of northwestern Saskatchewan and northeastern Alberta. They were promised a rational railroad system in order to move their agricultural products to market and bring in farm machinery, building materials and fuel. They feel, and rightly so, that they are paying exorbitant freight rates.
As an example of the situation let me refer specifically to the 38-mile gap in the rail line between Lindbergh, Heinsburg and Frenchman Butte, Saskatchewan. If that gap were filled 328 miles could be cut from the round trip between Heinsburg and Saskatoon. I brought this situation to the attention of the house before I had been a member of parliament for a month. I brought it to the attention of the railway experts in Montreal. They indicated they had no intention of completing this line unless I could show them how they could make money. They suggested that money could not be made because there was not a sufficient amount of freight to be hauled. They also indicated to me that they received additional money because of hauling freight the extra 328 miles. By the closing of this gap the farmers of that area would save a great deal of money. It would also effect a saving because boxcars would no longer have to be shunted in Edmonton at a cost of $11.70 per car. The railway indicated that was the cost some nine years ago and I am sure it has not gone down since.
The former administration took a step in the right direction a few years ago when the two rail lines to which I referred were built. That was an experiment which paid dividends. I see no reason why the building of other new lines would not have the same result.
There are tremendous deposits of natural resources in that area. Several years ago I indicated to hon. members that there is enough salt under the prairie lands around Lindbergh to last the human race for 1,000 years. I am glad to see that no one in the house is roaring with laughter over that statement. There is a vast vein of salt, of the table variety, in that area. It is believed to be from 88 to 250 feet deep and stretches for 350 miles. It encompasses an area about the size of Ireland.
In the area where the Peace river runs through the south end of Wood Buffalo Park there is a cliff of solid crystal gypsum. It is 100 feet high and stretches for approximately 17 miles. No one knows how far back it

February 7, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Bigg reaches. No one is particularly worried because there is enough gypsum in that cliff to fulfil construction requirements to rebuild every building in the world without even scratching the surface of that deposit.
In spite of all these natural resources our railway experts sit in Montreal biting their nails trying to balance their budgets. I suggest they cannot balance their budgets because they are lacking vision, guts and imagination. These experts should have some of the courage and imagination which brought people to these areas of our country. These people still hope that some day we in Ottawa will wake up and fulfil the promises made when they moved to these areas.
Nine years ago I promised these people that if the government would not complete this 38 miles of line I would go out and build it myself. I hope I will not have to leave this place to do so but I am a man of my word and I intend to hammer at the government until something is done. If the present government will not keep this promise I shall work harder to put the previous administration back in office. I am sure such an administration would do something about this situation rather than spending its time with the railway experts worrying about which lines should be abandoned.
Over a period of six years I have been talking about building a dirt road to McMurray. Both the provincial and federal authorities have said that the road cannot be built economically because there are not enough people in the area. However, when Sun Oil of Pennsylvania decided to develop the tar sands and spent $69 million on a pilot plant someone decided there were resources in northeastern Alberta and built a road.
The young people of this country are beginning to think we in Ottawa are nothing but a bunch of old fogies who spend our time fighting each other, looking for scandal and running each other down. They say that if they were in Ottawa things would be different. We are busily training these young people to think. It is a dangerous experiment if we think we can sit here and keep them out of public life. The way the red guard is acting in China is nothing compared to what will happen here unless we smarten up, and I do not think our young people will give us 20 years to do so. They want action and they want it now. If we are to provide free education we had better provide also work and opportunity. If we do so I am sure we will not have to worry about a brain drain to the

south. Great opportunities exist in Canada but our young people are not getting the advantage of them. This is our fault. It is the fault of those who were frightened by the depression as a result of which they lost their vision. If that vision has not been lost it has been seriously dimmed in the last five years.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I was proud to be a member of parliament nine years ago and I am still proud to be a member of parliament but, like my friend who just spoke, I want to know when we are going to give up the dull habit of arguing and go back to the old habit of acting. I think that 1967 would be a very good year in which to act at least as much as we talk. If the government is short of ideas, I and others on this side of the house have them. If the administration is tired and has lost its vision, let it not worry. Hon. members on the government side said ten years ago that we could not form a government which would accomplish things, but we did.
I close my remarks by reminding the house again of the three figures which I think are significant. I believe they should be a warning to the present administration. If in five short years we were able to change a deficit of $700 million a year to a figure of $1,300 million on the blue side of the ledger, we can do it again. I admit that the job will be three times as hard because now we are $2 billion behind. However, we on this side of the house have men who know how to do it and who have had some practice. They did it once and they can do it again.
I do not necessarily want to wait for an election. Perhaps it will not come for a year or two because the government is being well supported by hon. members on my extreme left. So I beg the present government to start acting now. If it is too tired, we are willing to take over any time; if it is not too tired then let us have a few results. If it does not have ideas itself, let it ask us. Let us have a parliamentary committee working with dedication, and I do not mean the kind of dedication which is found in history books; I mean the kind of dedication which ends up on the blue side of the ledger in the bank. This is the only kind that has any real appeal for the people of this nation who are becoming very restless indeed.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the mini-budget debate we are continuing
February 7, 1967	COMMONS
today proves to us once again that the government is unable to administer the country adequately and democratically, according to the wishes of Canadian taxpayers; otherwise, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) would not have had to bring down this so-called baby budget which will be fraught with consequences for the Canadian taxpayers.
The Minister of Finance does not seem to realize that the heaviest burden of the government rests on his own shoulders; as a matter of fact, he has to face problems which are all the more serious as he is attempting to carry out his duties in a modern age with antiquated, obsolete and out-of-date methods.
The government is aware that older people, for instance, need more income in order to meet the steadily increasing cost of living. After numerous pressures from all quarters, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) agreed to increase the old age security pension, but one soon realizes that the purchasing power of those people will in no way increase when all the taxes announced in the present budget will come into effect. As a matter of fact, not only will the old people not get more goods and services and not be paid more than before but the purchasing power of all the others will also be reduced because of higher taxes.
The minister and his parliamentary secretary have tried and are still trying to convince the people that in order to make some under-privileged classes a little more affluent, a little more must be taken away from the workers, those who toil, those who transform and develop the country. That is unfair, in my opinion, because I know that what the older people were asking for was economic freedom, the freedom to choose the things they need to live decently the remainder of their lives.
We are capable of supplying the elderly with all they need without depriving any member of the Canadian community. The old people mainly require food, lodging, clothing, medical care and recreation, goods and services which we can produce and supply in abundance without depriving anyone.
Why then, must we deprive younger men and women through taxes in order to provide for our senior citizens? Why not simply lay down an up-to-date accounting system that would truly reflect the actual wealth of the country? Earthly goods were created to meet the physical needs of the whole human race,
The Budget-Mr. Laprise not only for the few or for certain classes of people. All need not enjoy the same degree of prosperity but all should at least be able to satisfy their basic needs. The means and methods of acquiring wealth are legitimate inasmuch as they are organized to this end. They are evil or distorted to the extent that they defeat this purpose. We know that Providence has placed upon this earth, especially perhaps in Canada, in one form or another, all that is required, with man's co-operation and, naturally, with an adequate social structure, to meet the essential needs of all human beings. The old people as well as Canadian families still have unsatisfied needs. As a result of the constant increase in the cost of living, the average income is inadequate to provide a decent standard of living.
And what about those with a low income or no income at all? They are dispossessed in the midst of plenty; they are dispossessed in the midst of undeveloped natural resources which we fail to transform into natural wealth.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that the government can no longer govern according to the wishes of our society. But we are organized into a society and every well-organized society exists for the benefit and welfare of its members.
But because of an out-dated, obsolete economic system, many members of our society do not benefit from the advantages our Canadian society has to offer. Can we blame our methods of production, our industrialists, our farmers, our workers, our transport services, our teaching and health services? Not at all.
The whole problem lies in our distribution system. Available goods and services do not meet the needs of the members of our society. That is why everything goes wrong. That is why there is so much discontent and so many strikes of all kinds. That is the reason for so much undue hardship and for the imbalance in our distribution system. It does not serve its purpose.
Our economic system is not social, it does not allow each and every member of our society to enjoy the earthly goods provided for their welfare. According to the very words of His Holiness Pope Pius XI:
For then only will the economic and social organism be soundly established and attain its end when it secures for all and each those goods which the wealth and resources of nature, technical achievements and the social organization of economic affairs can give.
12750	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Laprise
And he adds, still in the encyclical Quadragesima Anno:
These goods should be sufficient to supply all needs and an honest livelihood and to uplift men to that higher level of prosperity and culture which, provided it be used with prudence, is not only no hindrance but is of singular help to virtue.
Then, it is recognized everywhere-at least I hope so-that production will attain its end only when it reaches the consumers, all consumers, and we must not stop or slow down the production of goods and services until all the needs of every member of our Canadian community have been met.
If the government keeps on operating through loans at the pace we have known since confederation, we shall never be able to celebrate our second centennial. If the government continues to tax the small wage earners, the poor, the have-nots, in order to give them a hand-out in social welfare from time to time, before 25 years we will live under a system of state socialism.
And to all those who would like to depend upon the state to fully ensure their wealth or their goods, I say that they would be well advised to consider the fate of our Indians in Canada. When we see how the government is managing the assets of the Indians, we are not inclined to try it out.
The system of private property and free enterprise has been able to supply goods and services in abundance. It is our responsibility to see that those goods and services attain their end, consumption.
To do that, it is necessary to have a modern economic system which meets the needs of our time. If our present economic system leads us to constant indebtedness, to the loss of private property, let us change it and follow the monetary system based upon the real value of our production and our productivity.
Let us adopt a monetary system that will allow a profit on production, although the ultimate objective of production should not be profit, but the fulfilment of man's needs. Profit is a tried and true incentive. Removal of this incentive altogether would jeopardize the output and would thus hurt consumers by forcing hardship upon them.
We need a system capable of maintaining the profit incentive and ensuring, at the same time, an adequate sharing and distribution of goods and services produced, thus serving the interests of both producers and consumers.
Only the Creditistes are proposing such a system and have been doing so for a long

DEBATES	February 7, 1967
time. As a matter of fact, it was submitted to this house when I was only 10 years old. At that time, right in the middle of the depression, the social credit proposals were laughed at and Canadians were starving from coast to coast in the midst of plenty. People were starving while food was destroyed and production stopped. The Creditistes continued to advocate their monetary system during the war; however, our war effort was not financed by social credit but by social debit, so that at the end of the war we had a debt of $18 billion.
The Creditistes continued to ask for a monetary reform. They were still laughed at. But although this is peacetime, we have a deficit of $27 billion. And that is not the end. The minister keeps on borrowing more, mortgaging our future even more. He keeps on taxing Canadians, dispossessing them even more to the benefit of high finance.
My colleague the hon. member for Vil-leneuve (Mr. Caouette) puts it very well when he says:
The big ones grow bigger in smaller number and the small ones get smaller in larger number.
That is the result of a debt money system, a false system.
Money and credit being a title and a call to production of any kind, the total amount of money and credit to be applied to production must be truly proportional to the volume and price of the total production realized or realizable on demand. That is why Social Credit feels that money is based on all the production existing or immediately possible, meeting the needs of the consumers and not on the selfish motives of some profiteers, such as the private controllers of money and credit.
Since, in modern society, you can have goods and services only if you can pay for them, then all members of society must have a minimum amount of money in order to get a minimum amount of goods and services.
Nowadays, money is obtained through salaries, dividends, social security measures and inheritances. This distribution does not, as we know, affect all members of society; therefore, another way must be found to guarantee each member of society a share of the goods offered.
This is one of the reasons why the Creditistes advocate the payment of periodical dividends to everyone from the time he is bom until he dies. Many problems, today more than ever, stem from the fact that salaries do not give workers the purchasing power
February 7, 1967

necessary to buy the necessities of life for their families and themselves, and this brings about repeated demands for higher wages and a whole series of strikes. But each wage increase is accompanied by an increase in the price of goods, new taxes on production and sales, which are added to the price of the goods. Wages, therefore, can never keep up with prices and, as a result, we always have this inadequate purchasing power. The Social Credit answer to this problem is the national dividend, which would increase purchasing power without affecting production costs, and the compensated discount which lowers prices without prejudice to manufacturers. This would supplement the income of consumers and enable them to purchase the goods they want.
With modern production techniques, automation as we call it, we no longer have to fear a dearth of goods, unless we really want it that way. It is becoming easier all the time to produce with less work, and this production must be brought within the reach of consumers. The only way to do this is to give them adequate purchasing power.
Economists, businessmen and labour leaders now admit what we have been advocating all along. Mr. Robert Theobald, a British economist with the United States government, says that we must separate the concept of work from that of remuneration, adding that each citizen should, as a matter of admitted and constitutional right, be assured of a minimum income during his whole life.
I should like to quote Mr. J. Fenwick, vicepresident of O.F.L., who said:
Automation endangers our traditional concept of a salary as remuneration for work. A new means to distribute purchasing power must be found.
May I also quote Mr. Gilles Endicott, director of research with the United Packinghouse Workers Union. According to Mr. Endicott:
Automation requires that we change our fundamental notion that wages must correspond to the work accomplished. However revolutionary this may seem, and even though it is contrary to the Calvinist moral code, we have accepted the principle that income should not necessarily be related to work.
Such statements confirm what we have been advocating. Since production is made easier through automation, we should adjust our financial system to achieve maximum production and consumption. We cannot do more and we should not do less.

The Budget-Mr. Laprise
We cannot and should not shirk progress which frees man from labour. There is obviously only one solution to the problem. If we want to keep the machines, we must develop a method whereby workers will be paid for the work performed in their stead by machines.
Income should be determined by the amount of wealth produced and not by the amount of work done. To distribute unpurchased wealth, we advocate the establishment of a national dividend, so that this wealth surplus can be distributed.
The establishment of a national dividend is not only feasible, it is justified from a moral point of view: it is required by justice. The increase in wealth resulting from a common effort represents collective and not individual earnings. This increased value due to a collective effort through automation and development of nuclear energy today fills up our store-houses to full capacity and it is the result of individual independence and skilfulness.
In the remote past, man worked alone, he was independent of his fellow-men, but he did not produce much. When he came out of his isolation, his production increased, but at the expense of his independence. When he tilled his own land, raised his own sheep, weaved his own fabric, he was a workingman independent of his fellow-men. But when he was torn away from his land to be assigned to special tasks and closely connected with his fellow-men, he had to give up his independence. He took to shoemaking perhaps, but others were weaving for him, tilling the soil for him. He no longer could be self-sustaining. His production capacity increased but he was just as poor as before. All he was getting-I am referring to workers in general-was a living allowance. The first theft was perpetrated at that time.
However, when the advent of the machine age reduced his work to the 20th part of a pair of shoes, he lost both his ability as a craftsman and his self-reliance. All he kept was his livelihood. Although his production kept on increasing afterwards, his livelihood, and nothing more, remained his sole reward. Uneasiness increased along with theft. And finally, when machines reached a state of perfection, and automation made its appearance, man had lost everything: independence, manual skill and his livelihood. He had to accept hand-outs and the theft was consummated.
February 7, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Deachman
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
This surplus of wealth is a collective inheritance after all. It does not belong to anybody in particular. It results from life in society and it depends upon it.
The national dividend is an alternative to sabotage. It eliminates vexation, disarms the social rebel and brings class struggle to an end. It provides encouragement to collective work and fosters social fellowship. It enables us to foresee a huge growth of our basic liberties for the future, crowning political liberty with labour liberty.
The dividend makes a free man of every individual.
